The Biden-era Coalition for Health AI (CHAI) exemplified everything wrong with DC's approach to innovation—letting corporate giants rig the system under the guise of "oversight." When Big Tech funds the very groups setting AI standards, it's not governance—it's regulatory capture. The Trump administration's move to dismantle this crony framework restores sanity: let hospitals compete on real results, not their ability to lobby bureaucrats.

Biden's HHS turned healthcare AI into a closed shop for Silicon Valley and mega-hospital chains, freezing out innovators who couldn't afford the pay-to-play fees. Now, by scrapping CHAI's gatekeeping, the feds are forcing a shift from credentialism to merit—where tools prove their worth in clinical outcomes, not compliance with some tech cartel's checklist.

This isn't about deregulation; it's about stopping the weaponization of "ethics" by monopolists. When CMS pilots AI prior auth systems, the metric should be patient wait times slashed—not how many ex-Google execs sit on the oversight board. The swamp loses when progress is measured in lives improved, not committee seats filled.
